doc.title: Roscoe Mitchell interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, May 23, 2023

chapter: Army, Chicago and the new music
title: Working with Muhal rather than talking about breaking boundaries
summary: Asked about late-night talk of changing the music, he says the work was rehearsing and writing for Muhal, who urged finishing pieces and wrote a Fats Waller-style piece.

story.theme_name: Chicago: the jazz migration and its clubs
story.community_name: Going north: working the Chicago jazz scene

blocks.x: I want to ask you about that but sometimes I get this vision in my head when I hear music that is sort of breaking boundaries. I picture gentlemen like yourselves when you were younger sitting around in a late night diner talking about what we could do to make the music different. And I asked that sort of question to Rashied Ali and he answered, “No we never really talked about it we just did it. The guys I was hanging out with we didn’t sit down and say now we’re going to play in or we’re going to play out or no bar lines, it was just something we did spontaneously.” Does that ring a bell with you?

Well not really. I mean you know because stepping over to Muhal’s arena you know, you’re working man. You’re working. You’re being encouraged. You know if you bring a piece in and you’re having some problems with it you were encouraged to go home and change whatever you wanted to do and bring your piece back because Muhal used to always say, you know, “You need to get it right you know, because if you don’t every time you listen to it you’re going to hear an unfinished part there” so like I’m saying you were encouraged to do these things and then having a big band to write for, yeah man, Muhal was writing these pieces like Fats — you know, Fats Waller — the stride piano. He would spend — you know I was in college at that time and I’d leave college and go right over to Muhal’s house and then be there you know until the evening and stuff, and he would still come to — and I wasn’t the only one there you know — he would still come to the rehearsal on Monday with a new piece you know. So yeah there was differences between Chicago and the style, you know, how the music developed. So, but yeah, nine times out of ten we were there working on the music.
